Julien was already cold and haughty. He gave thanks, but in very vague terms that committed him to nothing. Could it really be possible, he said to himself, that I am the natural son of some great lord exiled to our mountains by the terrible Napoleon? At every moment, this idea seemed less improbable to him... My hatred for my father would be proof of it... I would no longer be a monster!

A few days after this monologue, the Fifteenth Hussar Regiment, one of the most brilliant in the army, was drawn up in battle formation on the parade ground at Strasbourg. Monsieur the Chevalier de La Vernaye rode the finest horse in Alsace, which had cost him six thousand francs. He had been commissioned as a lieutenant without ever having been a second lieutenant except on the rolls of a regiment of which he had never heard.

His impassive manner, his stern and almost malicious eyes, his pallor, and his unalterable composure began to establish his reputation from the very first day. Soon afterward, his perfect and measured courtesy, and his skill with pistols and weapons, which he made known without too much affectation, discouraged any thought of joking aloud at his expense. After five or six days of hesitation, the prevailing opinion in the regiment declared itself in his favor. There is everything in this young man, the old, mocking officers said, except youth.

From Strasbourg, Julien wrote to M. Chélan, the former curé of Verrières, who was now approaching the utmost limits of extreme old age.

       *       *       *       *       *

“You will have learned, with a joy of which I have no doubt, of the events that have led my family to enrich me. Here are five hundred francs, which I beg you to distribute quietly, without any mention of my name, to the unfortunate, poor now as I once was, whom you no doubt assist as you once assisted me.”

       *       *       *       *       *

Julien was intoxicated with ambition and not with vanity; nevertheless, he devoted a great deal of his attention to outward appearance. His horses, his uniforms, and his servants’ liveries were maintained with a correctness that would have done honor to the punctuality of a great English lord. Having been a lieutenant, by favor, for barely two days, he was already calculating that, in order to be commander in chief by the age of thirty at the latest, like all the great generals, he had to be more than a lieutenant at twenty-three. He thought only of glory and of his son.

It was in the midst of the transports of the most unbridled ambition that he was surprised by a young footman from the Hôtel de La Mole, who arrived as a courier.

       *       *       *       *       *

“Everything is lost,” Mathilde wrote to him, “come as quickly as possible, sacrifice everything, desert if necessary. As soon as you arrive, wait for me in a hired carriage near the small garden gate, at No. ... in the Rue ... I shall come and speak to you; perhaps I shall be able to get you into the garden. Everything is lost, and I fear beyond remedy; rely on me, you will find me devoted and steadfast in adversity. I love you.”

       *       *       *       *       *

Within a few minutes, Julien obtained leave from the colonel and set out from Strasbourg at full gallop; but the dreadful anxiety consuming him did not allow him to continue traveling in this fashion beyond Metz. He threw himself into a post-chaise; and it was with almost incredible speed that he arrived at the appointed place, near the small garden gate of the Hôtel de La Mole. The gate opened, and at once Mathilde, forgetting all regard for propriety, flung herself into his arms. Fortunately, it was only five in the morning, and the street was still deserted.

“Everything is lost; my father, fearing my tears, left on Thursday night. Where for? No one knows. Here is his letter; read it.” And she got into the hired carriage with Julien.

       *       *       *       *       *

“I could have forgiven anything except the plan to seduce you because you are rich. There, unhappy girl, is the dreadful truth. I give you my word of honor that I shall never consent to a marriage with this man. I shall guarantee him an income of ten thousand livres if he is willing to live far away, beyond the borders of France, or, better still, in America. Read the letter I have received in reply to the inquiries I had made. The insolent fellow had himself urged me to write to Mme de Rênal. I shall never read a line from you concerning this man. Paris and you fill me with horror. I urge you to shroud what is to happen in the deepest secrecy. Frankly renounce a vile man, and you will regain a father.”

       *       *       *       *       *

“Where is Mme de Rênal’s letter?” Julien asked coldly.

“Here it is. I did not want to show it to you until you had been prepared.”

    LETTER

“What I owe to the sacred cause of religion and morality compels me, Monsieur, to take the painful step I am now taking with you; an infallible rule commands me at this moment to harm my fellow man, but in order to avoid a greater scandal. The pain I feel must be overcome by the sense of duty. It is only too true, Monsieur, that the conduct of the person about whom you ask me for the whole truth may have seemed inexplicable or even honorable. It may have been thought proper to conceal or disguise part of the reality; prudence required it, as did religion. But this conduct, which you wish to know about, was in fact extremely reprehensible, and more so than I can say. Poor and greedy, it was by means of the most consummate hypocrisy, and by seducing a weak and unhappy woman, that this man sought to establish himself and become somebody. It is part of my painful duty to add that I am obliged to believe that M. J... has no religious principles whatsoever. In all conscience, I am forced to think that one of his means of succeeding in a household is to seek to seduce the woman who has the greatest influence there. Cloaked in an appearance of disinterestedness and in phrases from novels, his great and sole object is to contrive to gain control of the master of the house and his fortune. He leaves behind him unhappiness and everlasting regrets,” etc., etc., etc.
